lead: This unit builds the language of engineering thermodynamics: how to choose a system, describe its state, and recognise equilibrium. After it you can classify systems, read property and process diagrams, state the zeroth law, and compute boundary work with a clear sign convention.
about: The unit starts with two ways of looking at matter: microscopic and macroscopic (1.1). It then fixes the bookkeeping: a system and its boundary (1.2), properties that define a state, and paths, processes and cycles (1.3). Equilibrium and the quasi-static process (1.4) make a process drawable as a line. The zeroth law (1.5) gives temperature and thermometry. Work and heat (1.6) are boundary transfers, not properties, with a fixed sign convention. Displacement work and other work modes (1.7) turn the convention into integrals such as ∫p dV. The chapters build from vocabulary to measurable quantities, so later units can apply the first and second laws.

chapters.idea: Thermodynamics can be studied by tracking molecules or by using bulk measurable properties.
chapters.depth: Cover the domain of thermodynamics, the microscopic (statistical) view that follows molecules, and the macroscopic (classical) view that uses bulk measurable properties such as pressure p, volume V and temperature T. Explain why engineering uses the macroscopic view: too many molecules, averages are enough. Some syllabi call this the microscopic and macroscopic points of view. Mention the continuum idea briefly. Keep statistical formulas out.

figure.aria: A tree splits thermodynamic views into microscopic, which tracks molecules and uses statistics, and macroscopic, which uses measured bulk properties p, V and T.

chapters.example: A copper block has mass 1.00 kg and volume 1.12×10⁻⁴ m³. Is density a microscopic or macroscopic property? Calculate its density.
chapters.trap: Saying pressure is only microscopic; pressure is a macroscopic property that comes from molecular collisions.
chapters.leave: Molecular kinetic theory and statistical mechanics derivations; detailed property tables are in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A system is the chosen region, and its boundary decides what mass and energy cross.
chapters.depth: Define system, surroundings and boundary. Classify closed (control mass: no mass crosses, energy may), open (control volume: mass and energy may cross), and isolated (no mass, heat or work crosses). Distinguish rigid, adiabatic and diathermic boundaries by what crosses. Mention steady state only as a running condition where properties at a point do not change with time; equilibrium is Chapter 1.4. Some syllabi call an open system a control volume.

figure.title: System and boundary
figure.aria: A block diagram classifies systems as closed with no mass crossing but energy allowed, open with mass and energy crossing, and isolated with no mass, heat or work crossing.

chapters.example: A rigid tank holds 2.0 kg of air. A valve opens and 0.50 kg of air escapes while 30 kJ of heat leaves the tank. Take the tank as the system. Does mass cross the boundary? Does energy cross it? Is the system closed or open?
chapters.trap: Closed is not the same as isolated: a closed system can exchange heat and work. Open means mass crosses; it does not require flow work to be taught yet.
chapters.leave: First law for open systems and steady flow energy equation to Unit 2; equilibrium to Chapter 1.4.

chapters.idea: Properties fix a state; a path through states is a process, and a closed path is a cycle.
chapters.depth: Define property, state, state point, path, process and cycle. Classify intensive (p, T), extensive (V, U, m) and specific (v = V/m) properties. For a simple compressible system, two independent intensive properties fix the state. Cover cyclic and non-cyclic processes. Explain that properties depend only on state, while heat and work depend on path; detailed path transfers come in Chapter 1.6. Some syllabi call specific properties per-unit-mass properties.

figure.aria: A directed graph shows state 1 going to state 2, state 2 to state 3, and state 3 back to state 1, forming a cycle.

chapters.example: A gas goes from state 1 (p = 100 kPa, V = 0.20 m³) to state 2 (p = 200 kPa, V = 0.10 m³), then back to state 1. Is 1→2→1 a cycle? What is the net change in volume after one complete cycle?
chapters.trap: Work and heat depend on the path; volume, pressure and temperature depend only on the state. Calling heat a property loses marks.
chapters.leave: Quasi-static path to 1.4; work and heat as path transfers to 1.6; property tables and equations of state to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Equilibrium means no unbalanced driving force; a quasi-static process moves through near-equilibrium states.
chapters.depth: Define thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium; a system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when none of these change with time. Distinguish equilibrium from steady state: steady state can have flow through, with gradients fixed. Define quasi-static process as one slow enough to pass through near-equilibrium states, so it can be drawn as a continuous line on a state diagram. State that quasi-static is not automatically reversible. Some syllabi call it quasi-static or quasi-equilibrium. Keep reversible and irreversible definitions for Unit 3.

figure.title: Quasi-static path
figure.aria: A block diagram shows a slow small step passing through near-equilibrium states from state A to state B, while a fast change has no continuous path.

chapters.example: A gas is taken from state 1 (p₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 0.20 m³) to state 2 (p₂ = 200 kPa, V₂ = 0.10 m³) along a quasi-static path with pV = constant. Check whether p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Can this path be drawn as a continuous line on a p–V diagram?
chapters.trap: Quasi-static does not mean reversible; a slow process with friction is still irreversible. Equilibrium is not the same as steady state.
chapters.leave: Reversible and irreversible processes, entropy and Carnot cycle to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The zeroth law defines temperature as the property that is equal in thermal equilibrium.
chapters.depth: State the zeroth law: if A is in thermal equilibrium with C and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Define temperature as the property equal when thermal equilibrium is reached; heat flows only when temperatures differ. Cover empirical temperature, thermometric property, Celsius and Kelvin scales, T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15, ice and steam fixed points, and the gas thermometer in outline. Some syllabi call it the concept of temperature and principles of thermometry.

figure.aria: A graph shows body A and body B each in thermal equilibrium with a thermometer C, so the dashed edge marks that A and B are also in thermal equilibrium.

chapters.example: A thermometer reads 25.0 °C in body A and 25.0 °C in body B. Body A and body B are then placed in contact. Using the zeroth law, find the direction of heat flow and convert 25.0 °C to kelvin.
chapters.trap: Temperature is not heat. Equal thermometer readings mean no net heat flow; the zeroth law does not say the bodies have equal internal energy.
chapters.leave: Thermodynamic temperature scale and second law to Unit 3; detailed thermometer calibration to physics labs.

chapters.idea: Work and heat are energy transfers across a boundary, not properties, and their signs must be fixed before calculation.
chapters.depth: Define work as energy transfer by a force moving its point of application; define heat as energy transfer because of a temperature difference. State the engineering sign convention used here: Q > 0 when heat enters the system, W > 0 when work leaves the system. Define adiabatic boundary (no heat) and diathermic boundary (heat may cross). Give units J and kJ. Mention path dependence; do not derive the first law. Some syllabi call these heat and work interactions.

figure.title: Sign convention
figure.aria: A block diagram shows positive heat entering the system from the left and positive work leaving the system to the right.

chapters.example: A system receives 50 kJ of heat and does 20 kJ of work on the surroundings. Take heat added as positive and work done by the system as positive. Write Q and W with signs, then find the net energy transfer Q − W.
chapters.trap: Mixing conventions: if work done on the system is taken positive, the sign of W flips. State the convention before substituting numbers.
chapters.leave: First law, internal energy and enthalpy to Unit 2; entropy and second law to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Displacement work is the area under a p–V path, W = ∫p dV, and other work modes follow force × displacement patterns.
chapters.depth: Define displacement or boundary work for a quasi-static process: W = ∫p dV from V₁ to V₂. For constant pressure, W = p(V₂ − V₁). Explain sign: expansion gives positive work by the system, compression negative. Show p–V area. Cover other work modes at recognition level: spring/elastic W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²), where k is spring constant and x is extension; electric W = ∫V dq, where V is potential difference and q charge; surface tension W = ∫γ dA, where γ is surface tension and A area. Some syllabi include compression, elastic, electric, magnetic and surface tension work; only a few universities examine all derivations. Keep units consistent.

figure.aria: A plot of pressure against volume shows a horizontal line at 200 kPa from volume 0.10 to 0.25 m³; the area under it is the displacement work.

chapters.example: A gas expands quasi-statically at constant pressure 200 kPa from V₁ = 0.10 m³ to V₂ = 0.25 m³. Find the displacement work W = ∫p dV and state its sign.
chapters.trap: Using p in kPa and V in m³ gives work in kJ, not J. For compression, p dV is negative, so work done by the system is negative.
chapters.leave: Isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic work to Unit 2; shaft work and flow work to Unit 2; detailed electromagnetic work to physics.
